claims.text: Integrating metadynamics-guided free-energy mapping into alloy processing enhances phase stability relative to conventional processing.
Integrating metadynamics-guided free-energy mapping into alloy processing refines the microstructure relative to conventional processing.
Integrating metadynamics-guided free-energy mapping into alloy processing optimizes material properties relative to conventional processing.
Metadynamics can quantify free-energy barriers for phase transitions and map the relevant free-energy landscape.
A computed free-energy landscape can be used to design controlled alloy-processing routes.
Severe deformation, controlled temperature, and rapid processing can incorporate metadynamics insights into practical alloy processing.
Processing designed from free-energy information modifies the physical free-energy landscape and thereby guides phase transitions.
Guiding phase transitions through the free-energy landscape produces a more uniform and refined microstructure.
Knowledge of phase-transformation barriers permits processing parameters to be tailored for simultaneous phase stability and microstructural refinement.
Simultaneous phase stability and microstructural refinement optimize mechanical and functional properties.
Metadynamics-guided processing will produce finer grains and a more controlled phase distribution than conventional processing.
Metadynamics-guided processing will improve strength, ductility, or corrosion resistance relative to conventional processing.
Conventional processing strategies commonly increase strength at the expense of ductility.
Conventional thermomechanical routes may refine grains without concurrently enhancing phase stability.
The effectiveness of metadynamics-guided processing varies with alloy composition and processing scale.
The magnitude of improvement in complex multiphase alloys at industrial scale is uncertain.
The magnitude and cross-alloy generality of the predicted property improvements require experimental verification.
X-ray diffraction can assess phase distribution and phase stability in the proposed comparison.
Electron microscopy can measure grain size and microstructural uniformity in the proposed comparison.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in phase stability, refinement, and properties would falsify the hypothesis.
